title: New Mexico and El Paso Spent Millions on Climate Plans. Three New Data Centers Could Undo Them.
author: Paul Ratje
content:
Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to
address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse
gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in
Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar
ambition.

Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into
account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both
places.

Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the
largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by
Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on
another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.

A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive
from the Meta site, on [the Fort Bliss Army
post](https://elpasomatters.org/2026/04/30/fort-bliss-data-center-water-
electricity-use-army-carlyle-group-meta-project-jupiter/) in east El Paso.

The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very
meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist
Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters.

The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the
country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence
services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn [intense
scrutiny](https://elpasomatters.org/2025/09/19/project-jupiter-data-center-
santa-teresa-approved-dona-ana-commissioners/) in [recent
months](https://elpasomatters.org/2025/10/15/meta-el-paso-texas-data-center-
water-electricity-borderplex-alliance/), as residents and elected officials
have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household
electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are
either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according
to [research by The Texas
Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/02/texas-data-center-
information-lookups/).

But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which
encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable
because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers,
each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas
emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than
two million cars in a year.

They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen
oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and
Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants
at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state
regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively
impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said
Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University
of California, Riverside.

“The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said.

Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two
different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing
climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’
impacts separately.

“We've never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe,
director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what
we've had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.”

The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project
happening minutes away from them.

Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate
change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state
law; Texas has not.

![A truck sprays water across a dusty, wide-open excavation site with cranes
and mountains visible in the background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/pratje_propublica_datacenters_001_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)A
truck sprays water for dust suppression at the construction site of Project
Jupiter in Santa Teresa, New Mexico.

New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of
Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in
northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose
noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site,
even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.

Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project
Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the
state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate,
Silva said.

“This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit
something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the
job of the federal government?”

Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local
governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a
part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered
Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment
in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more
technology companies to the region.

State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas
legislators[ approved a data center sales tax
break](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/04/08/texas-data-centers-sales-tax-
break-billion-dollars/), which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on
equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion
in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.

New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break
for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing
large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity
using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as
microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires
electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by
2030.

The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large
amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate
change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s
data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions
annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring
Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases [in
2019](https://www.elpasotexas.gov/assets/Documents/CoEP/Government/Strategic-
Plan/Climate-Action/El-Paso-Climate-Action-Plan-English-Version.pdf). (The
Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s
not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)

“This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar
Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M
University. “This is a huge source.”

![An aerial view shows a massive industrial construction site with large
building foundations and steel frameworks set across a wide desert
landscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/pratje_propublica_datacenters_026_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)
![An aerial view captures a sprawling desert community with roads cutting
through sparse terrain, scattered homes and mobile residences leading toward
distant mountain ranges.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/pratje_propublica_datacenters_024_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)

Homes in Chaparral, New Mexico, sit adjacent to Meta’s data center, just over
the state border in El Paso, Texas.

### An Unprecedented Amount of Energy

Silva, the New Mexico representative, was initially [supportive of Project
Jupiter](https://elpasomatters.org/2025/09/16/project-jupiter-santa-teresa-
data-center-state-representatives/), in part seeing it as an opportunity to
create long-term jobs. Last year, she [voted in
favor](https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/25%20Regular/votes/HB0093HVOTE.pdf) of
a [bill that included an
amendment](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/behind-scenes-deals-
mexico-
paved-035900179.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAF_di2tbUTybKT6Oak7dXy6TZdqJ5hnWojcx2kF3gv835XR7t_WTI-p9c3LzlqxEA1ICzucByTcuWAzURL_x6G_HFTI5MV2tnNnCzuwQYM9-TOBQe0sc0XcVuE732tKHE8jcJ9kkLh3Wx9pDxcViFrpTgHY5oViFWixFsXprK71B)
— tacked on by state Sen. Michael Padilla, a Democrat from Albuquerque — that
allows facilities like Project Jupiter, which aren’t connected to the local
power grid, a 20-year exemption from clean energy laws, allowing them to
generate all their electricity with fossil fuels.

“We worked this bill pretty much the entire session, but it did not quite get
done. So, we found a piece of legislation that was very similar,” Padilla said
in an interview last year. “That’s the legislative process. You have to be
very creative to get your work done.”

But Silva soon soured on the project out of concern that it won’t employ
enough local workers and because it won’t rely on zero-emission renewable
energy. Oracle has said the data center will have 750 full-time employees when
it’s up and running. The company told Doña Ana County officials in early
September that nearly 3,700 people had worked at the site during construction
up to that point.

Silva and other state lawmakers have said they voted for Padilla’s bill
without realizing the broader implications for a data center project in the
southern part of the state.

“State regulators, state legislators, I think, were so caught off guard at the
speed at which these hyperscale data centers showed up in all of our
communities almost simultaneously,” Silva said. “I would support a
moratorium.”

![A portrait of a woman with dark curly hair and glasses, wearing a red plaid
button-down shirt and blue jeans, standing outdoors in a desert landscape with
her hands on her hips.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/20260918-Ratje-
metadatacenter_sarahsilva__004_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)New
Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva was initially supportive of Project Jupiter but
has soured on the project over time.

The amount of energy Project Jupiter needs is unprecedented in the region: The
data center will receive electricity from an on-site power plant made up of
fuel cells built by a company called Bloom Energy. Bloom has said the plant
will have the ability to produce up to 2.45 gigawatts of electricity — enough
to power around 1.5 million homes and more than El Paso Electric has ever
supplied to its 465,000 residential and commercial customers at one time,
according to the utility’s corporate reports.

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, has specifically lauded
Oracle’s promise to use fuel cells for electricity instead of natural gas
turbines, which would have used more water and produced more air pollution.
However, an air permit — a state-granted license that authorizes industrial
facilities to emit a predetermined amount of pollution — would allow the fuel
cells to produce up to 8.8 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions per year.
Lujan Grisham didn’t address questions from El Paso Matters about the impact
of these additional climate emissions.

The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of
climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso
Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental
Protection Agency’s emissions factors. Nancy L. Seidman, a senior adviser with
the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nonpartisan nonprofit focused on energy
policy, confirmed the emissions estimate is sound.

"Regulators should weigh all emissions and other impacts like water usage,
noise and local air pollution, which can affect public health, when they make
decisions about data center projects,” Seidman wrote in an email to El Paso
Matters. “This is particularly important when projects are phased over time,
so that an accurate account can be made of the total, holistic impacts.”

The data center planned for Fort Bliss is expected to use 3 gigawatts of
electricity that would likely be supplied by natural gas turbines, according
to officials with the Department of Defense, who shared details with reporters
during a briefing in April. The Army has issued few other details about the
project because it is still in “exclusive negotiations” with the developer,
Carlyle Group, a large publicly traded private equity firm.

Carlyle Group did not respond to a request for comment.

“These are cities in terms of their electricity consumption,” Peskoe, of
Harvard Law School, said of AI hyperscale data center campuses such as
Oracle’s and Meta’s. The facilities are cropping up so fast that “the pace of
this and the scale of this — I think there's no real parallel, at least for
50, 60, 70 years, but probably ever for the U.S. power industry.”

Facilities in New Mexico seeking a state air permit are required by law to
disclose estimated amounts of air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions the
project will release. And the state Environment Department has spent months
evaluating Project Jupiter’s air permit application, which was submitted in
April. A spokesperson for the environmental department didn’t respond to
emailed questions.

By contrast, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality only requires
project developers to disclose information about pollutants that affect local
air quality, and not about greenhouse gas emissions, which are what contribute
to climate change.

So when El Paso Electric sought an air permit last fall for the Meta data
center’s natural gas power plant, the utility didn’t have to share estimated
greenhouse gas emissions. The Texas commission approved the permit 20 days
after it was filed, following an expedited review.

Meta directed questions about its data center’s power plant to El Paso
Electric. The electric company declined to share estimates of the plant’s
greenhouse gas emissions but said in a statement that the Texas environmental
commission had reviewed and authorized the Meta power plant “under a standard
permit, which is specifically for projects with limited and well-controlled
emissions.” The statement said the facility will “operate in compliance with
state and federal standards.”

A spokesperson for the agency said, “All Standard Permits have gone through
formal notice and comment procedures and have been adopted by the Commission
in a public meeting.”

These plants will be releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases even as
climate change has become increasingly evident in the El Paso metro area,
which sits where Texas’ westernmost boundary meets New Mexico and northern
Mexico. El Paso’s temperatures have risen faster than those of almost any
other city in the U.S. since 1970, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit
that quantifies climate shifts throughout the United States. Drought driven by
climate change has [amplified the
impact](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1352231025000044)
of [wind storms that fill the air](https://elpasomatters.org/2025/05/11/el-
paso-weather-dust-storms-wind-climate-change-impact/) in El Paso with
hazardous dust in the spring and summertime.

This year has been the hottest on record in El Paso through the first nine
months of 2026, according to the National Weather Service. Similar records
have been set across the state line in New Mexico.

“If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with
natural-gas-fired turbines — it's kind of like bringing back a lot of the
retired plants that were more dirty, like coal,” said DuBois, the New Mexico
state climatologist.

Fernando Berjano, El Paso’s climate coordinator, wouldn’t comment specifically
on effects resulting from the data centers in the region, but he said the
kinds of power plants tied to them produce greenhouse gases that will make it
harder for the city to meet its climate goals, as well as produce air
pollutants.

If emissions increase in the El Paso area, “that has an impact on air quality,
that has an impact on pollution,” Berjano said, “which is something that we
all know is not good.”

steel structures, heavy machinery and prominent yellow and red cranes set
against a mountain backdrop at dusk.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/pratje_propublica_datacenters_039_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=2560)Construction
at the Project Jupiter data center in Santa Teresa, New Mexico

### The Road Ahead for Data Centers

Although construction is already underway on the Project Jupiter and Meta data
centers, regulatory hurdles remain for both facilities. The public hearing on
the Project Jupiter air permit was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, but the New
Mexico Supreme Court delayed it when opponents filed lawsuits challenging the
state’s approval process and the facility’s use of groundwater.

The state Supreme Court last month lifted the stay. New Mexico more recently
appointed an examiner to preside over the hearing that would authorize the
facility’s emissions. Other legal challenges are making their way through the
court system.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still waiting for the state’s Public Utility
Commission to approve construction of the power plant planned next to Meta’s
data center, a decision that could come later this year.

Officials with both Project Jupiter and Meta have said they are taking steps
to help mitigate the climate effects of their projects and plan to develop
clean energy projects elsewhere to create new electricity sources and offset
the greenhouse gases their data center power plants will release. Oracle also
maintains that its emissions will be lower than what it sought in its air
permit application and that it plans to get to net zero greenhouse emissions
by 2031.

"Oracle is committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating
community feedback into our planning,” the company said in a statement.

![A crowd gathered under a covered outdoor pavilion holds up printed signs
with slogans like, "Don’t mess with our water," "Not in anyone’s backyard,"
and “El agua es vida.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/pratje_propublica_datacenters_053_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)Protesters
rally against the construction of data centers in their region.

The road ahead for data centers is unclear. Even once-supportive officials
have softened or changed course: Last year, Lujan Grisham, New Mexico’s
governor, said Project Jupiter “reaffirms New Mexico’s leadership in global
trade, advanced manufacturing, and digital infrastructure.” In Texas, Gov.
Greg Abbott at one point called his state “the epicenter of AI development.”

Now, amid growing opposition to Project Jupiter, Lujan Grisham [recently
said](https://sourcenm.com/2026/08/21/nm-residents-protest-pending-project-
jupiter-air-quality-permit-outside-environment-department/) she takes
seriously residents’ concerns about the data center “and expects any data
center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental
standards and use water responsibly.” This summer, Abbott [called on the Texas
Public Utility Commission](https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-
announces-puc-and-ercot-actions-protecting-residential-ratepayers-from-data-
center-costs) to ensure the projects pay for their own infrastructure and
don’t lead to higher electricity costs for residents. He also recommended [the
state Legislature
pass](https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/28225490/thomas-gleeson-pablo-
vegas-data-centers-directive-letter-to-puc-ercot-final.pdf) a number of
regulations related to data centers next year, many concerning water and
electricity usage, and recently [told the Texas Water Development
Board](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/14/texas-data-centers-abbott-
water-survey-enforcement/) to penalize data centers that do not report their
water usage.

Abbott’s new edicts do not address air pollution or climate change, nor the
effects that a data center project in one state can have on another.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Joe Moody, whose district includes much of west
and northeast El Paso, near two of the data center projects, said Abbott’s
proposals will likely shape the Texas Legislature’s debate over data-center-
related policies next year but called them just a starting point.

“In the governor’s directives, we’re not talking about local control and local
autonomy to make decisions on these projects,” he said. “And I do think that
that’s a whole other lane of conversation that we’re going to get into next
session.”
